title: Turing Machines and Computability
tagline: The Turing machine defines what computation means — and the halting problem proves there are questions no algorithm can ever answer.

sections.content:
In 1936, a 23-year-old Cambridge mathematician named Alan Turing published a paper that would define the limits of computation forever. He was not trying to build a computer — he was trying to answer a question in mathematical logic: can every mathematical statement be decided by a systematic procedure? His answer was no, and in proving it he invented the most influential thought experiment in computer science: the **Turing machine**.

A Turing machine (TM) is a strikingly simple device. It has a finite set of internal states, an infinite tape divided into cells that can each hold a single symbol, and a read/write head that moves left or right one cell at a time. On every step, the machine reads the symbol under the head, consults a finite table of rules, writes a new symbol, moves the head left or right, and transitions to a new state. That is the entire machine. No arithmetic unit, no memory hierarchy, no operating system — just a head, a tape, and a lookup table.

Yet despite this radical simplicity, the Turing machine can simulate **any algorithm** that has ever been devised. The **Church-Turing thesis** — the central claim of computability theory — asserts that the informal concept of 'an algorithm' is exactly captured by the formal concept of 'a Turing machine computation'. Every program you write in JavaScript, Python, or Rust is, in a precise mathematical sense, a Turing machine in disguise.

The dark flip side of this power is **uncomputability**. Because every possible Turing machine can be encoded as a string of symbols — making TMs into just another kind of data — you can ask a TM about other TMs. And some of those questions have no algorithmic answer, no matter how clever you are or how fast your hardware is. The **halting problem** is the most famous: given a program and an input, will the program ever stop running? Turing proved in the same 1936 paper that this question is unanswerable in general. This is not an engineering limitation. It is a mathematical absolute, as certain as the impossibility of dividing by zero.

sections.caption: Turing machine anatomy. The tape is unbounded (in the common textbook convention it extends infinitely to the right; two-way-infinite tapes are equally powerful). Each step: read the symbol under the head, look up the rule, write a symbol, move left or right, change state. The only ways to halt are entering q_accept or q_reject — the machine might also run forever.

sections.title: An Infinite Notepad with a Rulebook
sections.content:
Imagine you are working through a long calculation and you have two things: an **infinite notepad** with a cursor you can move left and right, and a **laminated rulebook**. The rulebook has a finite number of rules of the form: 'If you are in mood X and you see symbol Y under the cursor, write Z, move the cursor right, and switch to mood W'. Your 'mood' is the internal state. The notepad is your tape.

Now compare this to other computational models. A **finite automaton** has moods but no notepad at all — it must make all its decisions on the fly. A **pushdown automaton** (the model behind parsers and programming language grammars) gets a stack of scratch paper — but only a stack, meaning it can only read and write from the top. The TM gets the full notepad: read and write anywhere, in any order, as many times as needed. That extra freedom turns out to be the leap from 'powerful but limited' to 'can simulate anything'.

The **halting problem** translates naturally here: given someone else's rulebook and their initial notepad, can you figure out whether they will eventually put down the pen? You might watch them for a trillion steps and they are still writing. Are they going to stop? Will they write forever? You never know when to give up waiting. Turing proved that no rulebook — no algorithm — can answer this question for all possible combinations of rulebook and notepad.

sections.title: Formal Definition: The 7-Tuple
sections.content:
Formally, a **Turing machine** is defined as a 7-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject), where:

- **Q** is a finite set of **states** — the machine's internal moods.
- **Σ** is the **input alphabet** — the symbols that can appear in the initial input (does not include the blank).
- **Γ ⊇ Σ** is the **tape alphabet** — a superset of the input alphabet that also includes the blank symbol ␣ and any auxiliary symbols the machine uses during computation.
- **δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}** is the **transition function** — the rulebook. Given a current state and tape symbol, it returns a new state, a symbol to write, and a direction to move the head.
- **q₀ ∈ Q** is the **start state**.
- **q_accept ∈ Q** is the **accepting (halting) state**.
- **q_reject ∈ Q** is the **rejecting (halting) state**, and q_accept ≠ q_reject.

A **configuration** of a TM is a snapshot of its current situation: the state it is in, the entire tape contents, and the position of the head. The machine starts in configuration (q₀, tape holding the input followed by blanks, head on the first input symbol). It transitions from configuration to configuration via δ until it either enters q_accept (ACCEPT), enters q_reject (REJECT), or runs forever (LOOP).

This three-outcome system — accept, reject, or loop — is fundamentally different from the two-outcome world of finite automata. The possibility of looping is what introduces undecidability. If every TM always halted, every language recognised by a TM would also be decidable. The loop is the source of the mystery.

sections.title: What a Turing Machine Actually Computes: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Let us trace a small but illuminating example: a TM that decides the language L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ | n ≥ 0} — strings of n zeros followed by n ones. This cannot be decided by a finite automaton (it requires counting) but can be decided by a pushdown automaton. A TM gives us another, more mechanical approach: repeatedly cross off the leftmost remaining 0 and the leftmost remaining 1, until nothing is left.

State sequence (informal):
1. **q0**: look at the current cell. A `0` → overwrite it with X and go right (q1). A Y → all 0s are used up; go check that only Y's remain (q3). A blank → empty input, ACCEPT. A `1` → a 1 with no 0 to pair with, REJECT.
2. **q1**: move right over `0`s and Y's to the first unmarked `1`; overwrite it with Y and turn left (q2). Hitting a blank instead means a 0 has no partner: REJECT.
3. **q2**: move left over `0`s and Y's until reaching an X, then step right and return to q0.
4. **q3**: move right over Y's. A blank → ACCEPT; any leftover `1` (or `0`) → REJECT.

For input `0011`:
- Pass 1: `0011` → `X011` → `X0Y1`, walk back to the X.
- Pass 2: `X0Y1` → `XXY1` → `XXYY`, walk back.
- q0 now sees Y → q3 scans `YY` then a blank → ACCEPT.

For input `001`:
- Pass 1: `001` → `X01` → `X0Y`, walk back.
- Pass 2: `X0Y` → `XXY`; q1 skips the Y, finds a blank instead of a `1` → REJECT.

This multi-pass marking strategy is characteristic of TM algorithms. The ability to **re-read the tape, go backward, and use the tape as scratch space** gives TMs their power over automata and pushdown machines. The language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} — strings with equal numbers of three distinct symbols — further illustrates this: a PDA can only match two counts simultaneously, but a TM can mark all three with multiple passes.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The machine is literally the `delta` table plus a five-line loop — exactly the 7-tuple definition: states, tape alphabet {0, 1, X, Y, _}, transition function, start state q0, and accept/reject (reject = 'no rule applies'). It has no arithmetic unit: it 'counts' by pairing each 0 with a 1 on the tape, using X and Y — symbols in Γ but not in the input alphabet Σ — as scratch marks. The step limit is the simulator's concession to the halting problem: in general you cannot know in advance whether waiting longer would produce an answer.

sections.title: The Church-Turing Thesis: All Roads Lead to the Same Place
sections.content:
In the 1930s, mathematicians were hunting for a precise definition of 'computable function'. Three independent formalisms emerged almost simultaneously:

- **Alan Turing** (1936) defined Turing machines and called a function computable if a TM could compute it.
- **Alonzo Church** (1936) defined the **lambda calculus** — a formal system of function abstraction and application — and called a function computable if it could be expressed in lambda calculus.
- **Kurt Gödel** (building on Jacques Herbrand, 1931–34) defined the **general recursive functions**; Stephen Kleene's equivalent μ-recursive form builds every computable function on ℕ from zero, successor, and projections using composition, primitive recursion, and an unbounded search ('minimisation') operator.

Astoundingly, all three definitions turned out to be **exactly equivalent**. Every function computable by a TM can be expressed in lambda calculus and as a recursive function, and vice versa. This triple coincidence was too strong to be an accident. Church and Turing both proposed — and this is the **Church-Turing thesis** — that these formal definitions capture the informal intuition of 'a procedure that can be mechanically followed to completion'.

The thesis cannot be **proved** in a mathematical sense, because it equates a formal object (TM computation) with an informal concept ('algorithm' or 'effective procedure'). But its credibility rests on massive empirical evidence: every model of computation anyone has ever proposed — RAM machines, cellular automata (including Conway's Game of Life), quantum computers in the unitary-evolution-only sense, combinatory logic, register machines, PostScript, Prolog, JavaScript — computes exactly the same set of functions as Turing machines.

The practical implication: if you can write an algorithm for something in JavaScript, then in principle a TM could do it too, and vice versa. Your programming language is a Turing-complete formalism. The Church-Turing thesis is what makes 'computability theory' coherent — without it, the theory would be about one specific machine rather than a universal notion of computation.

sections.title: Encoding TMs as Strings: The Universal Turing Machine
sections.content:
A critical insight that makes the halting problem possible to even state is that **a Turing machine can itself be encoded as a finite string of symbols**. This is not surprising — your computer programs are files, and files are strings. The key move is recognising that we can therefore treat TM descriptions as just another kind of input.

Given a fixed encoding scheme, write ⟨M⟩ for the string encoding of machine M, and ⟨M, w⟩ for the encoding of M together with input string w.

Now consider a TM called the **Universal Turing Machine (UTM)**. The UTM takes as input ⟨M, w⟩ and **simulates** the computation of M on w. Whatever M would do to w, the UTM replicates. The UTM is the abstract precursor of the general-purpose stored-program computer — the idea that a machine's 'program' is just data that another machine can read and execute.

John von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report — written by someone who knew Turing's work well — described the practical version: the stored-program architecture, where code and data both live in the same memory. Every computer you have ever used is a physical instantiation of the UTM idea.

The UTM has one important limitation: **it inherits M's behaviour exactly**, including any infinite loops. If M loops on w, the UTM also loops. This is not a bug — it is the crux of why the halting problem is hard. The UTM cannot magically determine when M is about to halt; it has to actually simulate M step by step.

sections.title: The Halting Problem: Turing's Diagonal Argument
sections.content:
**The halting problem** is the language HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ | M is a TM and M halts on input w}. The question is: is HALT decidable? Does there exist a TM H that always halts and correctly outputs ACCEPT if M halts on w, REJECT if M does not halt on w?

Turing's proof that HALT is undecidable is one of the most elegant arguments in mathematics. It proceeds by **contradiction via diagonalisation**.

**Step 1:** Assume, for contradiction, that a decider H for HALT exists. H takes ⟨M, w⟩ and always halts, outputting ACCEPT or REJECT.

**Step 2:** Construct a new TM D (the 'diagonaliser') that takes a single input ⟨M⟩ (a machine's own encoding). D operates as follows:
- Run H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ (ask H: 'does machine M halt when given its own description?').
- If H says ACCEPT (M halts on ⟨M⟩), then D **loops forever**.
- If H says REJECT (M does not halt on ⟨M⟩), then D **halts and accepts**.

**Step 3:** Ask what happens when D is run on its own description ⟨D⟩:
- **Case A:** Suppose D halts on ⟨D⟩. Then H correctly says ACCEPT. But then D's rule says: loop forever. Contradiction.
- **Case B:** Suppose D does not halt on ⟨D⟩. Then H correctly says REJECT. But then D's rule says: halt. Contradiction.

Both cases lead to a contradiction. Therefore the assumption in Step 1 is false: **no such H can exist**. The halting problem is undecidable.

The argument is called **diagonalisation** because of its connection to Cantor's diagonal argument for the uncountability of the reals. You can visualise a giant table where row M and column w contains 'HALT' or 'LOOP'. Machine D is designed to differ from every row M at column ⟨M⟩ — it lies precisely on the diagonal and disagrees with every machine about what it does to its own encoding. The self-reference is the engine of the proof.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Assume decider H exists\nH(M, w) = ACCEPT if M halts\nH(M, w) = REJECT if M loops"] --> B["Build D:\nInput: description of M"]
    B --> C["Run H on (M, M's description)"]
    C --> D{"H says?"}
    D --> E["ACCEPT\n=> D loops forever"]
    D --> F["REJECT\n=> D halts"]
    E --> G["Run D on D's description:\nD halts? Then D loops. Contradiction!"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Contradiction => H cannot exist"]
sections.caption: Turing's diagonal argument. Machine D does the opposite of what H predicts when fed its own description. Running D on itself produces a logical impossibility, proving no decider H can exist.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The commented-out diagonal construction is the core of Turing's proof — it cannot run because `halts()` cannot exist. The step-budget runner is the honest alternative: it can confirm halting (a 'yes' is always trustworthy), but 'unknown' never safely becomes 'no' — `countTo(5000)` looks the same as `forever` after 1,000 steps. The Collatz example is a reminder that even tiny programs can have halting behaviour nobody has proved. This is why real analysers use timeouts, bounded model checking, and abstract interpretation — approximations, not exact deciders.

sections.title: Decidable vs. Recognisable: The Computability Hierarchy
sections.content:
Turing's analysis produces a fine-grained classification of problems:

**Decidable languages (Recursive):** A language L is decidable if there exists a TM M that always halts and correctly accepts every string in L and rejects every string not in L. 'Always halts' is the key. Examples: all regular languages, all context-free languages, the satisfiability problem for propositional logic with n variables (though the runtime is exponential), the problem of whether two DFAs accept the same language.

**Turing-recognisable languages (Recursively Enumerable, RE):** A language L is Turing-recognisable if there exists a TM M that halts and accepts every string in L, but may run forever on strings not in L. You get a guaranteed YES, but never a guaranteed NO — you just have to wait. HALT is RE: to check if (M, w) ∈ HALT, just simulate M on w. If M halts, we accept. If M loops, we loop — and we never output REJECT.

**Co-RE languages:** The complement of an RE language. A language L is co-RE if its complement (all strings NOT in L) is RE. HALT's complement — all (M, w) pairs where M does NOT halt on w — is co-RE. Crucially, it is not RE: there is no TM that always halts and accepts whenever M loops on w.

**Neither RE nor co-RE:** some languages cannot even be semi-decided in either direction. Examples: TOTAL = {⟨M⟩ | M halts on every input}, and EQ_TM = {⟨M₁, M₂⟩ | L(M₁) = L(M₂)}. No machine can reliably confirm membership, and none can reliably confirm non-membership.

The hierarchy is: Decidable = RE ∩ co-RE. HALT is in RE but not co-RE; its complement co-HALT is in co-RE but not RE; TOTAL is in neither. Below decidable lies the Chomsky hierarchy: decidable ⊃ context-sensitive ⊃ context-free ⊃ regular.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["All Languages / Decision Problems"] --> B["RE: Turing-Recognisable\n(TM halts on YES instances)"]
    B --> C["Decidable (Recursive)\n(TM always halts, YES or NO)"]
    C --> D["Context-Sensitive\n(linear-bounded automata)"]
    D --> E["Context-Free\n(pushdown automata)"]
    E --> F["Regular\n(finite automata)"]
    A --> G["co-RE\n(TM halts on NO instances)"]
    G --> C
sections.caption: The computability hierarchy. Decidable problems form the intersection of RE and co-RE. HALT is RE but not co-RE, hence undecidable. Below decidable, the Chomsky grammar hierarchy maps to automata classes. Problems outside RE entirely cannot even be partially recognised.

sections.title: Reductions: Proving Problems Undecidable
sections.content:
The halting problem is not the only undecidable problem — it is the **source** of undecidability for a vast range of problems. The technique is called **reduction**: to show problem B is undecidable, you show that if B were decidable, you could use it to decide the halting problem. Since HALT is undecidable, B must be too.

More precisely, problem A **reduces** to problem B (written A ≤m B) if there is a computable function f such that x ∈ A iff f(x) ∈ B. If A is undecidable and A ≤m B, then B is undecidable.

**Famous undecidable problems derived from HALT:**

- **The totality problem**: Does TM M halt on *every* input? Undecidable. (If we could decide this, we could solve HALT by constructing a machine that ignores its input and simulates M on w.)
- **Program equivalence**: Do two programs compute the same function? Undecidable. (Proved by reducing from HALT.)
- **The emptiness problem for TMs**: Does M accept any string at all? Undecidable. (Contrast: this is decidable for DFAs.)
- **Post Correspondence Problem (PCP)**: Given tiles with top and bottom string labels, can you arrange them so the top concatenation equals the bottom? Undecidable — a simple combinatorial puzzle that HALT surprisingly reduces to (any TM computation can be encoded as a set of tiles).
- **General static analysis of security properties**: Does program P ever read out of bounds, or ever reach line 42? Undecidable in general — a direct reduction from HALT (put the 'bad' action right after a simulation of M on w).

**Rice's Theorem** is the master generalisation: *any non-trivial property of the language of a TM is undecidable*. A 'property' here means a set of TMs closed under computational equivalence (if M₁ and M₂ accept the same language, they either both have the property or neither does). 'Non-trivial' means some TMs have it and some do not. The consequence: you cannot write a program that decides, for all programs P, whether P terminates on every input, whether P ever produces a specific output, or whether P computes the same function as a reference implementation — all non-trivial semantic properties. Behavioural questions that are not strictly about the input/output language — 'does P ever use memory after freeing it?', 'is P malware?' — are undecidable too, by similar reductions from HALT.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Rice's theorem does not say analysis is useless — it says every automatic analyser makes a trade-off. Sound type systems (Rust, OCaml, Haskell) never accept a type-incorrect program but reject some correct ones. TypeScript deliberately gives up soundness for JavaScript compatibility. Dynamic tools (tests, sanitizers, Valgrind) report only real problems but only on the paths you ran. Proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, or Dafny can establish deep properties of a specific program — but only because a human supplies the specification and much of the proof, so they escape Rice by not being fully automatic.

sections.content: **Historical context:** Alan Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem' addressed Hilbert's **Entscheidungsproblem** (decision problem): is there a mechanical procedure that decides, for any statement of first-order logic, whether it is logically valid? Alonzo Church had answered 'no' a few months earlier using the lambda calculus; Turing's independent answer came via the halting problem, and his machine model is what convinced people (Gödel included) that 'mechanical procedure' had finally been captured. His contemporary Kurt Gödel had already shaken mathematics with his **incompleteness theorems** (1931), proving that any consistent, effectively axiomatised formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements that cannot be proved within that system. Turing's result is closely related: there are computational questions whose answers exist in principle but cannot be found by any algorithm. The two results together define the boundary between what mathematics can formally capture and what lies beyond. A modern coda: the **Busy Beaver** function BB(n) — the most steps any halting n-state, 2-symbol TM can take — grows faster than any computable function. In 2024 the online bbchallenge collaboration proved BB(5) = 47,176,870, with the proof checked in Coq; BB(6) is already far beyond reach.

**Common interview and exam misconceptions to avoid:**

1. 'Undecidable means computationally hard (like NP-hard).' WRONG. Undecidable means no algorithm exists at all — not that the algorithm is slow. NP-hard problems are decidable (just slowly); undecidable problems have no solution regardless of time.

2. 'Quantum computers can solve the halting problem.' WRONG. Quantum computers are conjectured to be faster for certain problems (like factoring), but they do not compute any new functions — they are Turing-equivalent in the computability sense. The Church-Turing thesis covers quantum computation.

3. 'A Turing-recognisable language is almost decidable.' NUANCED. Being RE is a strong property — it means you can always confirm membership. But the lack of a guaranteed rejection can make RE languages practically useless for decision-making (you can never safely say NO).

4. 'Rice's theorem means we cannot analyse programs at all.' WRONG. It means we cannot do so perfectly and generally. Every useful static analysis tool is a carefully chosen approximation — unsound, incomplete, or limited in scope — and those approximations are valuable engineering achievements.

items: A **Turing machine** has a finite control (states + transition function) and an infinite tape (memory). The transition function reads one symbol, writes one symbol, moves left or right, and changes state. This minimal device can simulate any algorithm ever devised.

The **Church-Turing thesis** asserts that all reasonable models of computation — lambda calculus, recursive functions, RAM machines, real CPUs, any Turing-complete language — compute exactly the same class of functions. No stronger model of computation has ever been found.

The **Universal Turing Machine** takes a TM description ⟨M⟩ and an input w as its own input and simulates M on w — the mathematical foundation of stored-program computing. Every general-purpose computer is a physical UTM.

The **halting problem** (HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ | M halts on w}) is undecidable: Turing's 1936 diagonal argument shows that assuming a decider H exists leads to a contradiction. This is a mathematical absolute, not an engineering limitation.

A language is **decidable** if a TM always halts with a correct YES/NO answer. It is **Turing-recognisable (RE)** if a TM halts and accepts YES instances but may loop on NO instances. HALT is RE but not decidable; co-HALT is co-RE but not RE (decidable = RE ∩ co-RE); TOTAL is neither.

**Reductions** spread undecidability: to prove problem B is undecidable, show that deciding B would let you decide HALT. Direction matters: HALT ≤ B proves B undecidable. Program equivalence, totality, and the Post Correspondence Problem are all undecidable this way.

**Rice's theorem** is the master generalisation: any non-trivial semantic property of Turing machines (of what a program computes, not how it is written) is undecidable. This is the mathematical reason why perfect static analysis, bug detection, and security verification are impossible in general — every real-world tool is a principled approximation.

quiz.question: What does the Church-Turing thesis claim?
options: Turing machines are the fastest model of computation possible.
All programming languages are equivalent to pushdown automata.
Every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine.
The halting problem can be solved by quantum computers.
quiz.explanation: The Church-Turing thesis equates the informal notion of 'algorithm' with the formal notion of Turing computability. It cannot be proved mathematically (it bridges a formal object and an informal concept), but it is universally accepted: every proposed computational model computes exactly the Turing-computable functions.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the correct formal description of a Turing machine's transition function?
options: δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}, reading and writing a tape symbol and moving the head
δ: Q × Σ → Q, reading input but not writing
δ: Q × Γ → Q × {push, pop}, manipulating a stack
δ: Q × Q → Q × Σ, transitioning between pairs of states
quiz.explanation: The TM transition function takes the current state (from Q) and the current tape symbol (from the tape alphabet Γ), and returns a new state, a symbol to write on the tape, and a direction L or R to move the head. This is what distinguishes a TM from a DFA (which has no write and no head movement) and a PDA (which uses a stack, not a tape).

quiz.question: Turing's proof that the halting problem is undecidable relies on which technique?
options: Proof by induction on the number of states in the TM.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems applied directly to Turing machines.
Reduction from the NP-complete satisfiability problem (SAT).
A diagonalisation argument: assuming a halter exists and constructing a machine that contradicts its own output.
quiz.explanation: Turing constructs machine D: given any machine M, D asks a hypothetical halter H whether M halts on ⟨M⟩, then does the opposite. Running D on ⟨D⟩ produces a contradiction in both possible cases, proving H cannot exist. This is diagonalisation — D disagrees with every machine about its own self-referential behaviour.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a Turing-decidable and a Turing-recognisable language?
options: Decidable languages are finite sets; recognisable languages are infinite sets.
Decidable TMs always halt with ACCEPT or REJECT; recognisable TMs may loop forever on strings not in the language.
Recognisable languages are a strict subset of decidable languages.
Decidable languages require exponential time; recognisable languages run in polynomial time.
quiz.explanation: A decidable (recursive) language has a TM that always halts — you always get a YES or NO. A Turing-recognisable (RE) language has a TM that halts and accepts strings in the language, but may loop indefinitely on strings not in the language — you never get a reliable NO. HALT is RE but not decidable.

quiz.question: What does Rice's theorem state about Turing machines?
options: Any non-trivial semantic property of the language of a Turing machine is undecidable.
Every computable function can be computed in polynomial time.
Context-free languages are a strict subset of decidable languages.
The halting problem is solvable for all finite programs.
quiz.explanation: Rice's theorem: if P is any property of the language recognised by a TM (not of its mechanical structure), and P is non-trivial (some TMs satisfy P and some do not), then deciding P is undecidable. This eliminates the possibility of any general-purpose perfect program analyser.

quiz.question: The language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0} can be decided by a Turing machine but not by a pushdown automaton. Why?
options: A PDA cannot read the symbol 'c' from its input.
Context-free languages are not closed under concatenation of three symbols.
A PDA has only one stack and cannot simultaneously enforce three equal counts; a TM can mark symbols and make multiple passes.
A TM runs faster than a PDA, allowing it to handle more complex languages.
quiz.explanation: A PDA's single stack can match one pair of counts (e.g. a's with b's via push/pop), but cannot simultaneously verify that a third count (c's) equals both. A TM marks symbols on the tape in multiple passes — first matching an 'a' to a 'b', then matching that same 'b' to a 'c' — tracking all three independently.

quiz.question: The Universal Turing Machine (UTM) is significant because it demonstrates that:
options: Some TMs are more powerful than others and can simulate any TM.
A single fixed TM can simulate any other TM given that TM's description and input — the stored-program principle.
The halting problem is decidable for universal machines.
Quantum computers are equivalent to UTMs and can solve any problem.
quiz.explanation: The UTM takes ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates M on w — a single machine that can run any algorithm by reading the algorithm as data. This is the theoretical foundation of the stored-program computer: code and data in the same memory, with the CPU (UTM) interpreting the code as instructions.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of an undecidable problem?
options: Deciding if a string w is accepted by a given DFA.
Deciding if a context-free grammar generates an empty language.
Deciding if a given regular expression matches the empty string.
Deciding if two arbitrary programs always produce the same output on all inputs.
quiz.explanation: Program equivalence (do two programs compute the same function?) is undecidable by Rice's theorem — a direct consequence of reducing from the halting problem. The other three — DFA membership, CFG emptiness, and regex matching on the empty string — are all decidable problems with efficient algorithms.

quiz.question: Why is the complement of the halting problem (co-HALT) not Turing-recognisable?
options: Because if it were RE, then combined with HALT being RE, HALT would be decidable — but HALT is not decidable.
Because it requires a two-tape Turing machine to even describe.
Because complements of undecidable problems are always context-free languages.
Because co-HALT requires an infinite alphabet which no TM can use.
quiz.explanation: A key theorem: a language L is decidable if and only if both L and its complement are RE. HALT is RE (simulate M on w; accept if it halts). If co-HALT were also RE, then HALT would be decidable. Since HALT is not decidable, co-HALT cannot be RE. This means there is no TM that reliably accepts all (M, w) pairs where M does NOT halt on w.

quiz.question: A software company claims their new tool can perfectly detect ALL security vulnerabilities in any program without false positives or false negatives. What does computability theory say about this claim?
options: The claim is plausible if the tool uses machine learning with sufficient training data.
The claim is possible only for programs written in type-safe languages.
The claim is mathematically impossible: Rice's theorem proves any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable.
The claim is valid for programs under 10,000 lines, where exhaustive testing is feasible.
quiz.explanation: By Rice's theorem, 'does this program have a security vulnerability?' is a non-trivial semantic property of programs — and therefore undecidable. No algorithm can correctly classify all programs as safe or vulnerable without some combination of false positives, false negatives, or non-termination. Real security tools are sound approximations, not exact solvers.
